name: GAZ-64
hook: In 1941, a Soviet design team went from a blank page to a running four-wheel-drive scout car in just fifty-one days.
story: Picture Gorky, on the Volga, in February 1941. War is close, and the army wants a small car that can go anywhere. On the third of the month, engineer Vitaly Grachev and his team start drawing. Grachev already knows four-wheel drive. His group had built the GAZ-61, a four-wheel-drive passenger car. So they borrow what works. A 50-horsepower four-cylinder the factory already makes. Parts already coming off Soviet lines. And a brand-new frame of their own. Fifty-one days later, on the 25th of March, the little scout car rolls out for its first test. One magazine calls it the pygmy. From the outside it looks a lot like America's Bantam jeep. Underneath, it is home-grown. Production starts in August 1941, weeks after the invasion. Only a few hundred are built. But it leads straight to the GAZ-67, and to the BA-64 armoured car. Fifty-one days, and the idea was on the road.
description: The GAZ-64 was a light four-wheel-drive military scout car built by the Gorky Automobile Plant from 1941. A team led by engineer Vitaly Grachev developed it from the four-wheel-drive GAZ-61, using a 3.3-litre four-cylinder engine and other parts already in Soviet production, on a new frame. It resembled the American Bantam and Willys jeeps. Only a few hundred were made before the improved GAZ-67 replaced it, and it also formed the basis of the BA-64 armoured car.
